newsitem.title: CROATIA: IMF official cautions on CIS indebtedness.
newsitem.headline: IMF official cautions on CIS indebtedness.

text.p: Some former Soviet republics need to be wary of building up external debts and ensure their borrowing does not lead to a slowdown in the pace of reform, a senior IMF offical said on Friday.

John Odling-Smee, director of the International Monetary Fund's department dealing with the Baltic States and Commonwealth of Independent States, told a conference that private lenders should be careful about the debts, which have accumulated rapidly.
"Great care needs to be taken in external borrowing in these countries unless and until progress on economic reform can be seen to be very successful," he said.

Governments must not use foreign borrowing as a breathing space or excuse to ease up on reforms, Odling-Smee said. Apart from borrowing from the IMF and other institutions, many countries or smaller regions or cities have begun to issue international bonds.

"Care has to be taken not only by the borrowers themselves but also by the private financial markets which are increasingly coming in as lenders to replace international financial institutions and bilateral government lenders," Odling-Smee, director of the Fund's European II department, said.
Most of the countries in the region had little or no debt when the Soviet Union collapsed at the end of 1991 as Russia took over responsibility for Soviet debts.

By 1996, Georgia's external debt was 255.5 percent the value of its exports, making it severely indebted by World Bank classifications. Armenia, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan were classed as moderately indebted. Russia and Moldova followed them.

At the other end of the scale, Estonia's debt was only 9.4 percent of exports. But Odling-Smee said most countries in the region were pushing ahead with reform and that, for many, exports would increase and debts would not be as high in the future.
The Baltic States of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, advanced reformers with relatively low levels of debt, were not causing concern, he said.

Russia's external debt stood in 1996 at 126.4 percent of exports but Odling-Smee said this was not a problem. "Providing reforms move in a reasonable way in Russia, the external indebtedness is never going to be a serious problem."
Among the five states with highest debts, relative to their exports, most were also making progress on reform.
But he said the issue needed care because of the difficulty of the transition process, the risk and uncertainty associated wth the countries and the inexperiece of the borrowers.

Odling-Smee said the debts had built up as many countries had big fiscal problems, with falls in tax revenues, and had looked abroad for non-inflationary finance. Another key factor was the need to borrow to pay for energy imports.
